props.title: Live From Baghdad
props.initialSlug: CNN team risks all to cover first Gulf War live

sections.content: Live From Baghdad (2002) revolutionized how we view war journalism on film, joining the ranks of other powerful media-focused war films like The Year of Living Dangerously (1982) and Salvador (1986). Michael Keaton's portrayal of CNN producer Robert Wiener captures the frenetic energy of reporting during the Gulf War buildup, when CNN transformed from an upstart network into a global news powerhouse. The film's depiction of journalists operating under extreme pressure while navigating complex political relationships set new standards for depicting modern war correspondence.

sections.content: The film's authentic portrayal of war journalism builds on earlier classics like The Killing Fields (1984) and Under Fire (1983), but brings the story into the modern era of 24-hour news coverage. Director Mick Jackson captures the technological challenges of broadcasting from a war zone in 1991, with primitive satellite phones and constant negotiation with Iraqi officials. The relationship between Wiener and Iraqi Minister of Information Naji Al-Hadithi highlights the delicate dance between journalists and government handlers.

Live From Baghdad marked a shift in how war correspondence films handle objectivity. Unlike Good Night, and Good Luck (2005) or Broadcast News (1987), it shows journalists struggling not just with truth-telling but with being used as propaganda tools by both sides. The scene where Bernard Shaw and his crew broadcast during the first bombing raid revolutionized how we view real-time war coverage, predating similar moments in Control Room (2004) about Al Jazeera's Iraq War coverage. SUBHEAD: The Evolution of War Correspondence on Film

sections.content: While earlier films like Full Metal Jacket (1987) included war correspondents as secondary characters, Live From Baghdad puts journalism at the center of modern conflict. The film demonstrates how satellite technology and 24-hour news networks fundamentally changed war coverage, creating immediate worldwide impact that influences military and political decisions. This theme would later be explored in films like 5 Days of War (2011) and Whiskey Tango Foxtrot (2016).
